items.question: Why isn't my booking confirmed immediately?
items.answer: Because Cuban casas, drivers and guides confirm by hand, on their phones, within 24 hours.
items.details: Most of what we book has no reservation system. When you send a request, each provider gets it on WhatsApp or in their app and accepts or declines; you watch it in My trips. Nothing is charged until all of them say yes. Hotel allotments (Varadero) confirm instantly.

items.question: How do I pay, and what does it cost?
items.answer: Bank transfer (no fee), card or wallet (+ 3 %), or an invoice by wire. Prices are in euros.
items.details: Once hosts confirm you get an invoice and 48 hours to pay a 20 % deposit; the balance is due 30 days before departure (full payment if you book within 60 days). Your exchange rate is locked at the deposit. US-issued cards are declined by our European gateway; US travelers pay by wire.

items.question: How much cash should I bring?
items.answer: € 300–500 per person per week, in euros or Canadian dollars. Not US dollars, and no cards.
items.details: Visa and Mastercard do not work in Cuba. Budget € 15–25 a day for meals outside the casa, tips of € 5–10 a day for the guide, and small notes for taxis and markets. Split it between people and bags.

items.question: Do I need a visa for Cuba?
items.answer: Yes: an e-visa, applied for online 2–3 weeks ahead, plus the D'Viajeros form within 7 days of your flight.
items.details: Paper tourist cards ended on 1 January 2026. Approval usually takes up to 72 business hours; cost ≈ € 22–50 depending on nationality. Passport valid 6 months beyond return. We send a checklist with your dates and check your uploads.

items.question: Can US citizens travel with you legally?
items.answer: Yes, under one of 12 OFAC general-licence categories; you certify yours before paying.
items.details: Our trips are designed as a full-time schedule of activities with private hosts, which fits "Support for the Cuban People". We keep your certification 5 years and never book restricted state entities. Payment is by wire, outside the US banking system. Not legal advice; see the US travelers page.

items.question: What happens if there is a hurricane or a long blackout?
items.answer: Free date change or full refund if an official watch covers your dates; relocation and pro-rata refunds mid-trip.
items.details: June to November is hurricane season. If Insmet issues a watch or warning for your dates you choose a new date or a refund. Mid-trip we move you to safe stays, refund unused nights pro rata and give free rebooking within 12 months. Power cuts of 6–12 hours are normal and every stay we book has backup power.

items.question: What is a casa particular, really?
items.answer: A licensed room in a family home, with breakfast; the best way to meet Cubans and the backbone of our trips.
items.details: Every casa we book is visited: licence, backup power (generator, battery or solar), 24 h water storage, a host who answers within 30 minutes. You'll see bed type, bathroom, A/C and the exact backup on each stay card. Three tiers change the comfort, never the itinerary.

items.question: Can I change or cancel my trip?
items.answer: Change dates once for free; cancel with a fee that grows as departure nears.
items.details: More than 46 days out: full refund minus € 60. Then 10 %, 25 %, 40 %, 60 %, 80 % of the total is kept; under 24 hours, nothing is refunded. Refunds go to the original payment method within 14 business days. Force majeure is different: free change or full refund.

items.question: Is Cuba safe right now?
items.answer: Violent crime is rare; the real risks are shortages, outages and road conditions. Most governments advise increased caution, not against travel.
items.details: Canada and the US are at Level 2 (increased caution); France and the UK advise against non-essential travel because of shortages. We publish all four on the Current conditions page with dates, and our policy triggers if any is raised for your region.

items.question: How do I reach you from Cuba with bad signal?
items.answer: WhatsApp or Telegram when you have signal; the phone line always; your host or guide in person.
items.details: We check in every morning when the network is best. If you don't answer by midday your guide or host checks on you. The emergency line works on any network and is on your printed card.

sections.title: E-visa & entry
sections.lede: Four steps, start three weeks out
sections.note: Last verified 20 Sep 2026 against the consular portal · reviewed monthly

items.title: Check your passport
items.text: Valid at least 6 months beyond your return date. Children need their own.

items.title: Apply for the e-visa
items.text: Paper tourist cards ended on 1 Jan 2026. Apply on the official portal; approval usually within 72 business hours; single entry, 90 days, extendable once. Cost ≈ € 22–50 depending on your nationality and airline.

items.title: Complete D'Viajeros
items.text: Cuba's digital arrival form: passport, flight, address of your first casa (it's on your voucher), health declaration. Not earlier than 7 days before your flight. Save the QR to your phone and the offline kit.

items.title: At the airport
items.text: Show the e-visa code, the D'Viajeros QR, proof of insurance and your return flight. Keep € 300–500 in cash; nothing over the equivalent of US$ 5,000 undeclared.
Cuban-born travelers may need a Cuban passport or habilitación. Rules differ by case; tell us at booking and we'll point you to the consulate.

Entry to Cuba is the same e-visa. US law adds the travel-category certification: see the US travelers page. Note that an ESTA may be affected by a Cuba visit; check the US page before you book onward travel.
Links, a checklist with your dates, and a reminder 21 and 7 days out. Upload the approvals in Documents and we check them before you fly.

sections.title: Cultural etiquette
sections.lede: You're a guest in someone's home, and country
sections.note: Written with our hosts · reviewed yearly

items: Say good morning. Hosts register your passport in a book the first night; it's the law, not suspicion.
Water and power are rationed: short showers, lights off, phones charged when the grid is up.
Breakfast is generous and included; dinner at the casa is usually the best meal in town, order it in the morning.
Tip at the end, in cash, directly; it goes further than anything you can buy.
blocks.title: In the casa

items: Ask before photographing people, and show them the picture. Our hosts and guides have agreed to appear on this site; strangers haven't.
Politics: people will talk if they want to. Don't push, don't lecture, don't post about individuals.
Dress is relaxed but churches, ballet and family dinners expect shoulders covered and no swimwear.
Jineteros (street hustlers) are polite and persistent: a friendly "no, gracias" works.

items.text: "What's up?" The everyday greeting between friends.
"Mate", "friend". Informal, warm.
A licensed private home with rooms for guests.
A private restaurant, often in a family house.
A 1950s American car used as a shared taxi.
A bus. Pronounced "wa-wa".
Shredded beef in tomato and peppers; the national dish.

A power cut. You'll hear it daily; so will we.

sections.title: US travelers & OFAC
sections.lede: Legal travel to Cuba for US persons, step by step
sections.note: Last verified 30 Sep 2026 · not legal advice · reviewed with counsel quarterly

blocks.text: Under the Cuban Assets Control Regulations, US persons may only spend money on Cuba travel under one of 12 general-licence categories, whatever the booking channel or payment method. Tourism as such is not one of them. Vereda is a Spanish company; the rules still apply to you.

items.title: Pick your category
items.text: Most of our travelers use Support for the Cuban People: a full-time schedule of activities with private hosts, farmers, artists and guides, avoiding restricted state entities. Family visits, journalism, professional research, religious and humanitarian work are others. As of 30 Sep 2026 the people-to-people group category no longer exists.

items.title: Certify at booking
items.text: A short form before payment: category, your name as on the passport, a typed signature. We store it for 5 years as the law requires and give you a PDF.

items.title: Travel the schedule
items.text: Your itinerary is the schedule. Keep it, your receipts and your voucher for 5 years. We don't book GAESA or Gaviota properties, nor anything on the US restricted list.

items.title: Pay in euros, outside the US banking system
items.text: US-issued cards are declined by our gateway. Pay by international wire or invoice. No transaction is cleared in US dollars.

"Family visits" covers close relatives in Cuba. Our Family Visit package is built for it: airport transfers, a casa near your family, luggage for supplies, Spanish-speaking desk. Remittance and gift rules are separate; ask us.
A visit to Cuba can affect ESTA eligibility for some travelers to the US. Check the current State Department guidance before planning onward travel.

blocks.text: Three questions help you find a fitting category. If none fits, we'll say so rather than book you.

articles.title: Power outages in Cuba: what to expect and how we plan around them
articles.standfirst: Twenty-hour apagones are the baseline this year, not the exception. Here's what a cut looks like from inside a casa, what a generator does and doesn't run, and the four things we do before you arrive.
articles.author: Ana Rodríguez

photo.alt: Candle, power bank and coffee on a casa table during an evening apagón, Viñales
photo.caption: Evening at Casa Yamilé during a scheduled cut. The generator runs the fridge and fans; the candle is for atmosphere. Photo: Vereda, with permission.

blocks.text: Cuba's power plants are old, fuel is short, and demand peaks in the evening when everyone cooks. The national utility publishes a daily deficit and provinces take turns going dark. In 2025 the island had several total blackouts lasting more than a day; in 2026 planned cuts of 12 to 20 hours outside Havana are normal in the hot months.
None of this is a secret in Cuba. Your hosts plan their day around it: cooking early, charging phones when the light is on, keeping a torch by the bed. You will too, and it is easier than it sounds.

sections.title: What a cut looks like from inside a casa

blocks.text: Usually the schedule is known a day ahead; Yamilé will tell you at breakfast that the light goes at four. The fan stops, the fridge hums off, and the street gets quieter. If the casa has a generator it starts within a minute and the essentials come back. If it has a battery, the lights and the Wi-Fi router stay on but the air conditioning doesn't.

Evenings are the hardest part: it is hot, and there is less to do. Our travelers' tip, repeated in every review that mentions outages, is to be out. Dinner at a paladar with its own generator, music at the Casa de la Música, a walk along the Malecón. The casa is for sleeping, and a fan on a generator is enough for that.
Two nights without power, ten hours each. The generator kept the fan on and Ana messaged every morning. Honest, tiring, worth it. Knowing in advance is what made it OK.
blocks.cite: Marion T., Lyon · Viñales, February 2026 · verified review

sections.title: What a generator does and doesn't run

items.text: lights, fans, the fridge, phone charging, the router. Usually for 4 to 8 hours a night; fuel for generators is also rationed.
air conditioning in most casas, electric showers, kettles. Premium stays with 24-hour generators are the exception and cost accordingly.
quieter, no fuel, but smaller. Good for lights, charging and the router for 6 to 8 hours.
most casas use tanks heated when the grid is up. Shower early.

blocks.alt: Osvaldo starting the generator behind the casa

blocks.text: Every stay we book lists its backup explicitly: generator, battery, solar, or none. You'll see it on the stay card before you choose.

sections.title: What we do before you arrive

items.term: We only book stays with backup power
items.text: Verified on a visit: generator with fuel, battery, or solar. It's a filter on the listing and a line on every stay card.

items.term: We lend a 20,000 mAh power bank per room
items.text: And put a headlamp in your welcome kit.

items.term: We schedule the important things in the morning
items.text: When the grid and the signal are most reliable, and we check in with you by WhatsApp each morning while you're in Cuba.

items.term: If a cut runs past 12 hours and the casa can't cope
items.text: We move you (Hurricane Melissa in October 2025 was the rehearsal). Mid-trip disruption that costs you a night is refunded pro rata and you get free rebooking within 12 months.

items: Bring your own power bank too, and a torch. Charge everything whenever there's light.
Download the offline kit and offline maps before you fly; the router won't help when the tower is down.
Keep cash in small notes: card terminals don't exist and a shop without light still sells water.
Carry a printed itinerary and your emergency card. Paper doesn't need charging.
Ask your host about the schedule each morning, and plan the evening out.

blocks.text: Because the outage is also when the street comes alive: neighbours on the porch, dominoes under a single bulb on a battery, someone with a guitar. We won't romanticise it, Cubans don't, and it is a real hardship for the people who live with it every day. But if you understand the reality before you go, you can handle the inconvenience, and what you can't handle is being surprised. That sentence came from a traveler, and it is the whole reason this page exists.

about.title: Cuba is not a resort. It is a living culture.
about.lede: Travel with us to engage with Cuban families, artists and communities, not to consume a packaged holiday. We are transparent about the realities of travel in Cuba today: the power cuts, the fuel, the paperwork. We think that honesty is the beginning of trust, and the beginning of a better trip.

items.text: The total price before you click. The power schedule before you book. The 3-star review next to the 5-star one. Where every euro goes, on the invoice.
85 % or more of what you spend reaches Cuban families: casas, paladares, farms, guides and drivers. Guides keep their whole day rate. We publish the split per trip.
Named hosts, named villages, named traditions. "Bring € 300–500 in cash", not "bring sufficient cash". We say what we mean and we date it.

items.title: We stay with you
items.text: A Reality Briefing 30 days out, reconfirmation at 7 days and 48 hours, a WhatsApp check-in every morning in Cuba, and a phone line that answers in 15 minutes, day or night. If a storm or a blackout breaks the plan, we rebook, refund or relocate, and we say which within the hour.

vinales.lede: A valley of limestone mogotes where tobacco is still planted by hand and ox. You stay with families in the village, walk the red-earth tracks with a biologist, and learn how a leaf becomes a cigar from the people who grow it, not from a shop.

photo.alt: Osvaldo ploughing a tobacco field with oxen, mogotes behind

overview.title: What Viñales is, and isn't
paragraphs: The valley is a UNESCO cultural landscape and a working farm district of about 28,000 people. The village has one main street, a church square and a few hundred licensed casas; the valley has farms, caves and birds. Days are slow and early; nights are dark when the grid is down, and the stars are the compensation.

It is not a resort and not a theme park. Horse rides and farm visits are run by families who also farm; prices are set with them, and tipping the farmer directly is normal. Expect mud in the rainy season and dust in the dry one.

conditions.title: What it's like this month
conditions.updated: Updated Fri 3 Oct 2026 · sources: Unión Eléctrica, Insmet, our drivers

items.label: Power
items.text: Scheduled cuts of 6–10 h most days, usually afternoon and night. All our casas run a generator or battery for fans, fridge and charging.

items.label: Fuel
items.text: Normal this month on the Havana–Viñales road. Drivers confirm fuel 24 h before each leg.

items.label: Connectivity
items.text: ETECSA 4G in the village and at Los Jazmines; nothing in the valley. Download the offline kit before you leave Havana.

items.label: Roads & tracks
items.text: Autopista and the valley road are fine. The track to Cueva de Santo Tomás floods after heavy rain; guides check the morning before.

items.label: Weather
items.text: Hurricane season until 30 Nov; no watches active. 26–31 °C days, 19 °C nights in winter.

plan.title: How we plan around it
items: Casas chosen for backup power, 24 h water storage and a host who answers WhatsApp within 30 minutes.
A 20,000 mAh power bank lent per room; headlamps in the welcome kit.
Activities scheduled in the morning, when both the grid and the signal are most reliable.
If a casa drops out, three alternatives in the same price band within 24 h.

items.question: Is Viñales OK for someone in their seventies?
items.answer: Yes, with the right casa and pace. Choose a ground-floor room (three casas have them), skip the 8 km walk for the 3 km loop, and take the car to the viewpoints. Tell us and Daylin plans around it.
